dedupe_keys.name: san bruno natural gas transmission pipeline rupture and fire california 9 september 2010 ntsb investigation

description: On 9 September 2010 a 30-inch segment of Line 132, an intrastate natural gas transmission pipeline owned by Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E), ruptured in a residential area of San Bruno, California. The NTSB investigation page, read on 2026-09-26, records a crater about 72 feet long, the release of an estimated 47.6 million standard cubic feet of gas, and a fire that destroyed 38 homes and damaged 70; eight people were killed. The probable cause was PG&E's inadequate quality control during a 1956 relocation, which let a poorly welded pipe with a seam flaw be installed that grew until it failed during a pressure increase caused by electrical work at the Milpitas Terminal, and an inadequate integrity management programme. Exemptions of existing pipelines from pressure testing and the California Public Utilities Commission's weak oversight contributed, and the lack of automatic or remote valves and slow isolation made it worse. The page links the docket, report PAR-11-01 and recommendations to federal and state bodies, PG&E and industry associations. The page and report are free and in the public domain. Caveats: the case is a single US event. Simulation uses are pipeline failure, cascading effects and emergency response modelling for gas networks in urban areas. Related records: data-npms-national-pipeline-mapping-system maps US transmission pipelines.

name: San Bruno natural gas transmission pipeline rupture and fire, California, 9 September 2010 (NTSB investigation)
organisations: Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration
outcomes: The NTSB found poor 1956 quality control and weak integrity management as the probable cause, with regulatory exemptions from pressure testing and slow isolation contributing, and issued recommendations P-10-001 to P-11-032.
